claims.text: Severe lattice distortion and ordered interstitial complexes or short-range order are the primary factors governing increases in hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Lattice distortion and ordered interstitial structures impede dislocation motion.
Nanocrystalline grain structures provide additional Hall-Petch strengthening.
The proposed initial alloy is nanocrystalline and in an as-deposited state.
The proposed Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi- or W-based initial alloy exhibits significant lattice distortion.
Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi alloys can be synthesized with oxygen or nitrogen additions.
Adding oxygen or nitrogen during synthesis promotes the formation of ordered interstitial complexes.
Ordered interstitial complexes form within the distorted lattice.
Nanoscale grain boundaries are part of the structural mediator governing the mechanical response.
Interstitial dopants preferentially form ordered complexes that act as obstacles to dislocation glide.
Differences in constituent-element size and chemistry produce inherent lattice distortion.
Inherent lattice distortion contributes to solid-solution strengthening.
Ordered interstitial complexes, lattice distortion, and small grain size combine to increase hardness and strength.
The interstitial-doped sample will have greater hardness than the undoped baseline.
The interstitial-doped sample will have greater yield strength than the undoped baseline.
The doped alloy's ordered interstitial complexes will correlate with improved mechanical properties.
The proposed mechanism should operate in significantly lattice-distorted HEAs, including BCC alloys, when their microstructure permits interstitial ordering.
Coarse grains or crystal structures unfavorable to interstitial ordering can limit or alter the proposed mechanism.
The magnitude of strengthening depends on interstitial concentration and the efficiency of ordered-complex formation.
Interstitial strengthening may involve a trade-off with ductility.
